[[File:Cline cosmic ray mtg.jpg|thumb|David B. Cline, among other physicists, at a cosmic ray meeting in 1979]]
[[File:Cline 1979 cosmic ray mtg.jpg|thumb|Cline, among other physicists, in a salt mine. [Editor note: Most likely the site of a neutrino detector]]]
'''David Bruce Cline''' (December 7, 1933 – June 27, 2015) was an American particle physicist known for his contributions to the discovery of the [[Higgs boson]] and the W and Z intermediate bosons.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|title=David Bruce Cline|journal = Physics Today|volume = 69|issue = 7|pages = 69–70|doi=10.1063/pt.3.3243|year = 2016|last1 = Cousins|first1 = Robert D.|last2 = Rosenzweig|first2 = James B.|bibcode = 2016PhT....69g..69C|doi-access = free}}</ref> After receiving his Ph.D. from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], he went on to join the university's physics faculty and founded the "Pheno Group".<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Cousins|first1=Robert D.|last2=Rosenzweig|first2=James B.|date=July 2016|title=David Bruce Cline|journal=Physics Today|language=en|volume=69|issue=7|pages=69–70|doi=10.1063/PT.3.3243|issn=0031-9228|bibcode=2016PhT....69g..69C|doi-access=free}}</ref> Shorthand for [[Phenomenology (physics)|phenomenology]], the group consisted of [[Particle physics|particle physicists]] designing and running experiments alongside developing theoretical models that went beyond the current standard model of particle physics.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.pheno.wisc.edu/|title=Theoretical High Energy Physics: Phenomenology – The Institute For Elementary Particle Physics|language=en-US|access-date=2020-01-03}}</ref> He later moved to UCLA where he became a Distinguished Professor of Physics & Astronomy for his contributions to the growth of the UCLA Physics & Astronomy Department.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://senate.universityofcalifornia.edu/_files/inmemoriam/html/DavidB.Cline.html|title=David B. Cline|website=senate.universityofcalifornia.edu|access-date=2020-01-03}}</ref>

Rather than working in a U.S. based particle accelerator, the [[Superconducting Super Collider|Superconducting Supercollider]], Cline chose to work on [[CERN]]'s [[Large Hadron Collider]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://inspirehep.net/author/profile/D.Cline.1|title=Cline, David Bruce - Profile - INSPIRE-HEP|website=inspirehep.net|access-date=2020-03-16}}</ref> While there, he and others founded the [[Compact Muon Solenoid]] (CMS) experiment, which is still active today in investigating the Standard Model and is one of the largest international scientific collaborations in history.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://home.cern/science/experiments/cms|title=CMS {{!}} CERN|website=home.cern|access-date=2020-01-04}}</ref> Cline was also involved in the development of the [[ICARUS experiment|ICARUS]] [[neutrino detector]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=http://www.astro.ucla.edu/faculty/cline.htm|title=Prof.David Cline|website=www.astro.ucla.edu|access-date=2020-01-04}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1984/rubbia/biographical/|title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 1984|website=NobelPrize.org|access-date=2019-02-23}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> When assembled, it would be the largest detector of its time, built with the purpose of detecting neutrinos from the sun and the beams from CERN.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":0" />  

In the later part of his career, Cline shifted his interests towards astroparticle physics.<ref name=":0" /> He pioneered the use of liquified noble gases in particle detectors to enhance the detection through the use of a [[Time projection chamber|Time Projection Chamber]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/article/may-2011/eminently-noble|title=Eminently noble|last=Reardon|first=Sara|website=symmetry magazine|date=May 2011 |language=en|access-date=2020-01-04}}</ref> Not only did this facilitate work in investigating neutrino oscillations, the introduction of noble gases into detectors could be exploited to detect dark matter.<ref name=":4" /> Dark matter's elusive nature inspired Cline to organize a biannual international conference for dark matter research, which will go on to have its 14th meeting in March 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://conferences.pa.ucla.edu/dark-matter-2020/|title=Dark Matter 2020|website=UCLA Physics & Astronomy|access-date=2020-01-03|archive-date=2020-01-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200104013440/https://conferences.pa.ucla.edu/dark-matter-2020/}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Cline was born on December 7, 1933, in [[Rosedale, Kansas]]. He attended and graduated from Rosedale High School in the same city, and after being discharged from the army, attended [[Kansas State University]], where he received a BS in physics in 1959 and MS in physics in 1961 in physics.<ref name="pa.ucla.edu">{{Cite web|url=http://www.pa.ucla.edu/content/david-b-cline|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150710064803/http://www.pa.ucla.edu/content/david-b-cline|archive-date=July 10, 2015|title=David B. Cline {{!}} UCLA Physics & Astronomy|website=www.pa.ucla.edu|access-date=2019-06-27}}</ref>  He continued his studies and pursued a PhD at the University of Wisconsin - Madison under the guidance of Dr. William Fry.<ref name=":0" /> He completed his PhD thesis in 1965, titled "A Study of Some Rare Decay Modes of the Positive Kaon".<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cline|first=David Bruce|date=1965|title=A Study of Some Rare Decay Modes of the Positive Kaon|url=http://inspirehep.net/record/867098/}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> His PhD work investigated the existence of the then undiscovered electrically charged W boson and electrically neutral Z boson. His observations of decaying kaons dismissed the existence of the neutral weak force carrier,  but he would later go on to withdraw this belief when experiments at CERN claimed to require the existence of the Z boson for certain interactions.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
In 1967, Cline was appointed to the faculty at the University of Wisconsin.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cousins|first1=Robert D.|last2=Rosenzweig|first2=James B.|date=2016|title=David Bruce Cline|journal=Physics Today|volume=69|issue=7|pages=69–70|doi=10.1063/PT.3.3243|issn=0031-9228|bibcode=2016PhT....69g..69C|doi-access=free}}</ref> Once there, he co-founded the "Pheno Group", which consisted of physicists dedicated to pursuing a broad range of particle physics research in both theory and [[Phenomenology (physics)|phenomenology]].<ref name=":2" />

The same year, Cline began working at [[CERN]], and with [[Alfred E. Mann]] of the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and [[Carlo Rubbia]] of [[Harvard University|Harvard]], the team produced a document that launched the first experiments to study the weak force using [[neutrino]] beams at the new [[Fermilab]] accelerator complex.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cousins|first1=Robert D.|last2=Rosenzweig|first2=James B.|date=2016|title=David Bruce Cline|journal=Physics Today|volume=69|issue=7|pages=69–70|bibcode=2016PhT....69g..69C|doi=10.1063/PT.3.3243|issn=0031-9228|doi-access=free}}</ref> After a period of uncertainty, Cline and collaborators agreed with the claim coming from the [[CERN]] laboratory in Geneva that certain neutrino interactions required the existence of [[weak neutral current]]s.<ref name="pa.ucla.edu"/> In 1976, the group proposed upgrading the single-beam [[proton accelerator]] at CERN to a dual-beam [[Proton-Antiproton Collider|proton-antiproton collider]]. The installation of this 270 GeV antiproton-proton collider, along with the implementation of more advanced beam-cooling techniques, prompted the investigation for [[intermediate vector boson]]s (IVB). With a theorized mass of 80-90 GeV, it was expected that the high energy of the collider would lead to the first observations of these particles.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cline|first1=David|last2=Rubbia|first2=Carlo|date=August 1980|title=Antiproton–proton colliders and Intermediate Bosons|journal=Physics Today|language=en|volume=33|issue=8|pages=44–52|doi=10.1063/1.2914211|issn=0031-9228|bibcode=1980PhT....33h..44C}}</ref> The experiment at CERN proved successful, and in 1983 IVBs were detected and differentiated the weak force from the electromagnetic force for the first time.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /> The discovery warranted the 1984 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]], awarded to [[Carlo Rubbia|Dr. Carlo Rubbia]] and [[Simon van der Meer|Dr. Simon van der Meer]] for the discovery of the [[W and Z bosons]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1984/summary/|title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 1984|website=NobelPrize.org|language=en-US|access-date=2020-01-04}}</ref>

Following his involvement in the discovery of the W and Z boson, Cline moved to the UCLA Physics Department in 1986.<ref name=":3" /> Once there, he began actively pursuing efforts to grow the university's particle physics department and incorporate new areas of research. He was focused on hiring faculty with a specialization in accelerator physics, which was a rapidly growing field at the time.<ref name=":3" /> Cline became a distinguished professor of physics and astronomy for his contributions to the growth of astroparticle physics and accelerator physics with the support of the UCLA Physics & Astronomy department that gained him global recognition in the field. He proposed investigations into the mass of the [[Tau neutrino|ν<sub>Τ</sub>]] & [[Electron neutrino|ν<sub>e</sub>]] neutrinos using terrestrial solar and supernova neutrino sources, nucleon decay using the [[ICARUS experiment|ICARUS]] detector in Italy, and neutrino oscillations.<ref name=":4" /> To accomplish his projects, Cline and a small group of US physicists  proposed the new design of a supernova neutrino detector large enough to observe extra-galactic supernova bursts.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cline|first=David|date=November 1992|title=THE SUPERNOVA BURST OBSERVATORY: A PROTOTYPE EXTRA GALACTIC SN DETECTOR AND SUPERNOVA WATCH|url=https://lss.fnal.gov/archive/other/ucla-aph0062-11-92.pdf|journal=Fermilab Library}}</ref>

Cline was part of the experiment that made their discovery in 1983 at CERN which first implemented the scheme they proposed in 1976.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://home.cern/news/news/physics/carrying-weak-force-thirty-years-w-boson|title=Carrying the weak force: Thirty years of the W boson|website=CERN|access-date=2019-02-23}}</ref> Later Cline was also a member of the [[Fermilab]] experiment that discovered the [[top quark]] and of one of the [[CERN]] experiments that discovered the [[Higgs boson]] in 2012.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|title=The Telescope in the Ice|url=https://archive.org/details/telescopeinicein0000bowe|url-access=limited|last=Bowen|first=Mark|publisher=St. Martin's Press|year=2017|isbn=978-1-137-28008-4|pages=[https://archive.org/details/telescopeinicein0000bowe/page/96 96]–9}}</ref>

At UCLA he was also one of the pioneers of the use of liquefied noble gases as particle detectors and made innovative contributions to the development of the use of liquid argon and xenon to detect dark matter.<ref name="pa.ucla.edu"/>

In the early 1990s, the U.S. had plans to build the [[Superconducting Super Collider|Superconducting Supercollider]]. Cline was among many other U.S. scientists who chose to work on a competing European based supercollider, [[CERN]]'s [[Large Hadron Collider]] . He continued working at CERN's LHC and was a cofounder of the [[Compact Muon Solenoid]] (CMS) experiment. The goal was to detect and measure the stable particles that remain after colliding protons at nearly the [[speed of light]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Wolpert|first=Stuart|title=A Wondrous Machine to Unlock the Secrets of the Universe|url=https://www.physicalsciences.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/uclacernbigbang.pdf|journal=UCLA Physical Sciences}}</ref> in an effort to investigate physics beyond the [[Standard Model]] and identify the conditions of the early universe.

The [[Compact Muon Solenoid|CMS]] was constructed and is located at one of the four collision points that make up the LHC and is designed to detect [[muon]]s with high accuracy and be the most powerful solenoid magnet of its time, being capable of producing a magnetic field of 4 tesla.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cms.cern/detector|title=Detector {{!}} CMS Experiment|website=cms.cern|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref> The international collaboration that was CMS would come to be one of the largest of its kind, incorporating over 200 institutes and 50 countries.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://home.cern/science/experiments/cms|title=CMS {{!}} CERN|website=home.cern|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref> The collaboration proved to be successful, as the CMS was involved in the first 7 TeV proton-proton collisions, the discovery of the [[Xi baryon|Xi<sub>b</sub> baryon]], and the discovery of the Higgs Boson.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://labs.inspirehep.net/literature?sort=mostrecent&size=25&page=1&q=collaboration:CMS|title=INSPIRE|website=labs.inspirehep.net|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref> David Cline is listed as a contributor to these experiments for his contribution to the creation of CMS.

Cline was also involved in a collaboration between over 25 universities across the globe who proposed the construction of a neutrino detector in [[Fermilab]] in 2005. The proposed detector would be a 30 Kiloton Off-Axis Detector, with the purpose of studying  ν<sub>μ</sub> → ν<sub>e</sub> Oscillations in the [[NuMI]] Beamline.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Collaboration|first1=The NOvA|last2=Ayres|first2=D.|date=2005-03-30|title=NOvA Proposal to Build a 30 Kiloton Off-Axis Detector to Study Neutrino Oscillations in the Fermilab NuMI Beamline|arxiv=hep-ex/0503053|bibcode=2005hep.ex....3053T|language=en}}</ref> The NuMI Off-axis ν<sub>e</sub> Appearance, or NOvA, collaboration brings together over 240 scientists from 51 institutions to study the effects neutrinos may have had on the evolution of the universe<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://novaexperiment.fnal.gov/|title=NOvA|language=en-US|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>

== Notable Involvements ==

=== Super Proton-Antiproton Synchrotron & Compact Muon Solenoid ===
Although Cline is not credited for the discovery of the W and Z bosons, Cline and [[Carlo Rubbia|Rubbia's]] proposal of the installation of a proton-antiproton collider has led to advances in particle physics through the investigation of heavy bosons. Cline's role as a co-founder of the [[Compact Muon Solenoid|CMS]] experiment has also earned him the status of a contributor to the first 7 & 8 TeV proton-proton collisions, as well as the discovery of the Higgs Boson and Xi<sub>b</sub> baryon.

=== Investigation of Dimuon Events ===
In the early 70s, Cline investigated the production of dimuons from [[neutrino]]s and antineutrinos. These neutrino events require the generation and decay of [[Force carrier|intermediate particles]] that did not agree with models that predicted the intermediate particles to be heavy [[lepton]]s and [[Vector boson|semi-weak vector bosons]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Benvenuti|first1=A.|last2=Cline|first2=D.|last3=Ford|first3=W. T.|last4=Imlay|first4=R.|last5=Ling|first5=T. Y.|last6=Mann|first6=A. K.|last7=Orr|first7=R.|last8=Reeder|first8=D. D.|last9=Rubbia|first9=C.|last10=Stefanski|first10=R.|last11=Sulak|first11=L.|date=1975-11-03|title=Characteristics of Dimuons as Evidence for a New Quantum Number|journal=Physical Review Letters|language=en|volume=35|issue=18|pages=1203–1206|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1203|bibcode=1975PhRvL..35.1203B|issn=0031-9007}}</ref>

In February 1975, Cline and others reported on their observation of a new particle produced by high energy neutrino and antineutrino interactions. 14 dimuon events were observed, and due to the characteristics of the event and the absence of any trimuon events, the interaction seemed to require the presence of a new massive particle. The theorized particle, which was expected to have a previously unobserved [[quantum number]], would need to decay weakly in order to have two [[muon]]s in the final state.

The source of the second [[muon]] was argued to be due to the decay of [[pion]]s and [[kaon]]s. Cline and others provided evidence against this by observing "(i) the rate of dimuon events, (ii) the opposite signs of their electric charges, (iii) the different densities of the target materials in which they were produced, and (iv) the distributions in muon momentum and transverse momentum."

The neutrino interactions leading to dimuon events required the existence of a new particle that they called the y particle. The group theorized that, if the particle was a [[hadron]], the mass is between 2 and 4 GeV and the lifetime would have to be less than 10<sup>−10</sup>s. The alternate theory was that the [[neutrino]] interaction produced a neutral [[Lepton|heavy lepton]] that decayed into two muons and a neutrino/antineutrino.

=== Physics potential of a few 100-GeV mu+ mu- collider ===
Cline's most cited single-author paper describes the potential applications of " a few 100-GeV [[Antimuon|μ<sup>+</sup>]][[Muon|μ]]<sup>−</sup> collider". His proposal was inspired by the evidence that the [[Standard Model]] and [[Supersymmetry|SUSY]] Model should exhibit a [[Resonance (chemistry)|resonance]] at a mass just under 2[[Z-Boson|M<sub>z</sub>]]. At this energy range, it was very difficult to accurately detect and measure interactions at the [[Large Hadron Collider|LHC]]. Reaching such high energies was needed to search for the [[Higgs boson|Higgs]]. The μ<sup>+</sup>μ<sup>−</sup> collider would have also had applications in investigating TeV interactions with higher resolution than colliders at the time.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cline|first=David B.|date=October 1994|title=Physics potential of a few hundred GeV μ+μ− collider|journal=Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A: Accelerators, Spectrometers, Detectors and Associated Equipment|language=en|volume=350|issue=1–2|pages=24–26|doi=10.1016/0168-9002(94)91150-9}}</ref>

=== High-Transverse-Momentum Secondaries and Rising Total Cross Sections in Cosmic-Ray Interactions ===
While he was still at [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|UW - Madison]], Cline worked with [[Francis Halzen|Dr. Francis Halzen]] and studied [[hadron]] collisions from [[cosmic ray]] interactions. Their observations showed evidence for high-transverse-momentum secondaries in excess of the predicted exponential cutoff, which matched data from [[CERN]] at the time. Experiments at [[Intersecting Storage Rings|CERN ISR]] had shown that the [[Cross section (physics)|cross sections]] of hadron collisions had been larger than expected. The data supported the [[quark model]] of the [[proton]], where small momentum collisions would scatter at the "surface", leading to an exponential cutoff of the transverse-momentum. High momentum collisions, however, lead to interactions with the quarks and produce high-transverse momentum along with a [[Hadron|jet of hadrons]]. Their study concluded that the rise in the total cross section of the interactions of cosmic rays and the detection of hadron jets supports the theory of a [[Parton (particle physics)|composite model of the proton]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cline|first1=D.|last2=Halzen|first2=F.|last3=Luthe|first3=J.|date=1973-08-13|title=High-Transverse-Momentum Secondaries and Rising Total Cross Sections in Cosmic-Ray Interactions|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=31|issue=7|pages=491–494|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.31.491|bibcode=1973PhRvL..31..491C|issn=0031-9007}}</ref>

=== Observation of Elastic Neutrino-Proton Scattering ===
Cline spent time exploring [[Neutral current|weak neutral current]] interactions by scattering [[neutrino]]s by [[proton]]s. Previously, the exploration of this interaction was difficult due to the high neutron background and poor [[pion]]-[[proton]] separation. Cline mitigated these hindrances by using a detector that was sufficiently large enough to capture neutrino induced neutrons, which could be absorbed or detected through their interactions in the outer regions of the detector. Using a wide-band horn-focused neutrino beam at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]], Cline and others observed 30 events of neutrino-proton [[elastic scattering]], which gave results consistent with most [[Gauge theory|broken-gauge-symmetry]] models involving the [[Neutral current|weak neutral current]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cline|first1=D.|last2=Entenberg|first2=A.|last3=Kozanecki|first3=W.|last4=Mann|first4=A. K.|last5=Reeder|first5=D. D.|last6=Rubbia|first6=C.|last7=Strait|first7=J.|last8=Sulak|first8=L.|last9=Williams|first9=H. H.|date=1976-08-02|title=Observation of Elastic Neutrino-Proton Scattering|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=37|issue=5|pages=252–255|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.37.252|bibcode=1976PhRvL..37..252C}}</ref>

=== Experimental Observation of [[Plasma wakefield acceleration|Plasma Wake-Field Acceleration]] ===
At [[Argonne National Laboratory|Argonne National Laboratory Advanced Accelerator Test Facility]], Cline and group created a [[Plasma acceleration|plasma-wake field]] by exciting 21 MeV [[electron]]s through a dense [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] to measure the accelerated and deflected wake-field. This was one of the first instances of an experiment having performed a direct measurement of plasma wake fields by accelerating an injected witness-beam pulse in the wake of an intense driver-beam pulse in a plasma. They also demonstrated the existence of strong [[Transverse wave|transverse]] wake fields using the witness beam.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rosenzweig|first1=J. B.|last2=Cline|first2=D. B.|last3=Cole|first3=B.|last4=Figueroa|first4=H.|last5=Gai|first5=W.|last6=Konecny|first6=R.|last7=Norem|first7=J.|last8=Schoessow|first8=P.|last9=Simpson|first9=J.|date=1988-07-04|title=Experimental Observation of Plasma Wake-Field Acceleration|journal=Physical Review Letters|language=en|volume=61|issue=1|pages=98–101|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.98|pmid=10038703|bibcode=1988PhRvL..61...98R|issn=0031-9007|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1233868}}</ref>

=== The Search for [[Dark matter|Dark Matter]] ===
The XENON100 project was a large collaboration dedicated to finding dark matter particles that Cline was involved in. Conducted at [[Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso]] (LNGS) for 13 months during 2011 and 2012. The experiment featured an ultra-low electromagnetic background of (5.3 ± 0.6) × 10<sup>−3</sup> events/(kg day keVee) in the energy region of interest. The resulting data provided the most stringent limit for the mass of [[Weakly interacting massive particles|WIMPs]], m<sub>χ</sub>>8  GeV/c<sup>2</sup>, with a minimum [[nucleon]] [[Cross section (physics)|cross section]] of σ=2.0×10<sup>−45</sup>  cm<sup>2</sup> at m<sub>χ</sub>=55  GeV/c<sup>2</sup>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=XENON100 Collaboration|last2=Aprile|first2=E.|last3=Alfonsi|first3=M.|last4=Arisaka|first4=K.|last5=Arneodo|first5=F.|last6=Balan|first6=C.|last7=Baudis|first7=L.|last8=Bauermeister|first8=B.|last9=Behrens|first9=A.|last10=Beltrame|first10=P.|last11=Bokeloh|first11=K.|date=2012-11-02|title=Dark Matter Results from 225 Live Days of XENON100 Data|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=109|issue=18|article-number=181301|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.109.181301|pmid=23215267|arxiv=1207.5988|bibcode=2012PhRvL.109r1301A|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Detection of Energy Deposition Down to the KeV Region Using [[Scintillation (physics)|Liquid Xenon Scintillation]] ===
Cline was part of a collaboration to detect cosmic energy depositions in the KeV range in 1993. The group proposed a liquid xenon detector that could detect energies low enough to provide evidence for [[Weakly interacting massive particles|WIMPs]]. The proposed detector would also be able to distinguish [[alpha particle]]s from [[gamma ray]]s using [[Scintillation (physics)|scintillation]] and charge signal techniques. Previous detectors were not able to differentiate between background radioactivity and electrical noise, but by the utilization of an active chamber with high charge detection efficiency and liquid xenon scintillation, Cline and others suggested and believed that this type of detector would be the most effective method of directly measuring WIMPs.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Benetti|first1=Pietro|last2=Calligarich|first2=E.|last3=Dolfini|first3=R.|last4=Berzolari|first4=A. Gigli|last5=Mauri|first5=F.|last6=Montanari|first6=Claudio|last7=Piazzoli|first7=A.|last8=Rappoldi|first8=A.|last9=Raselli|first9=Gianluca L.|last10=Scannicchio|first10=D.|last11=Bettini|first11=A.|editor-first1=David B. |editor-last1=Cline |date=1993-10-19|title=Detection of energy deposition down to the keV region using liquid xenon scintillation|journal=Astroparticle Physics and Novel Gamma-Ray Telescopes|publisher=International Society for Optics and Photonics|volume=1948|pages=2–8|doi=10.1117/12.161382|bibcode=1993SPIE.1948....2B|s2cid=54622742}}</ref>

=== Detection of [[Primordial black hole|Primordial Black Holes]] ===
When [[primordial black hole]]s explode at the end of their life, they send a myriad of particles flying across the universe. In 1992, Cline set out to investigate how accurately the current models described the [[hadron]]ic and [[lepton]]ic spectrum of these bursts, and predicted values for the upper limit of the particle densities. He suggested methods to detect [[Gamma ray|gamma]] and [[neutrino]] bursts by utilizing the SuperNova Burst Observatory set to be constructed in New Mexico's [[Waste Isolation Pilot Plant|WIPP]] site.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cline|first1=David B.|last2=Hong|first2=Woopyo|date=December 1992|title=Possibility of unique detection of primordial black hole gamma-ray bursts|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|language=en|volume=401|pages=L57|doi=10.1086/186670|bibcode=1992ApJ...401L..57C|issn=0004-637X}}</ref>

== Published works ==

=== Papers ===
David B. Cline has over 1400 published papers, and is cited over 90,000 times in various journals for [[High-energy nuclear physics|high energy]] and [[Astroparticle physics|astroparticle]] physics. He participated in numerous collaborations including, but not limited to, the ICARUS project, CMS at CERN, and [[UA1 experiment|UA1]] collaboration. Below are some of the most cited and influential works that he contributed to.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://labs.inspirehep.net/authors/1013360|title=INSPIRE|website=labs.inspirehep.net|access-date=2020-01-15}}</ref>

=== Books ===

*''Weak Neutral Currents: The Discovery of the Electro-weak Force'', by David B. Cline. (Jan 1, 1997) {{ISBN|9780201933475}}
*''B/K Decays and Novel Flavor Factories,'' by David B. Cline (Editor) Published March 27, 1998 by [[American Institute of Physics]]. {{ISBN|9781563960550}}
*''CP Violation and Beauty Factories and Related Issues in Physics'', by David B. Cline (Contributor) and Alfred Fridman (Editor). Published Jan 1st 1991 by New York Academy of Sciences. {{ISBN|9780897666237}}
*''The Fourth Family of Quarks and Leptons First international Symposium,'' by David B. Cline (Contributor) and Amarjit Soni. Published Jan 1st, 1987 by New York Academy of Sciences. {{ISBN|9780897664356}}
*''Unification of Elementary Forces and Gauge Theories'', by David B. Cline. Published Nov 1st, 1980 by Harwood Academic Pub. {{ISBN|9780906346006}}

=== Articles ===
Cline wrote a total of seven articles for the [[Scientific American]] magazine. They are summarized below.

*''The Search for Dark Matter'', by David B. Cline, was an article published in the March 2003 issue of the Scientific American and David Cline's seventh and final contribution to the magazine. The article highlights the complexities in the search for [[dark matter]], and progress in its discovery.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-search-for-dark-matte/|title=The Search for Dark Matter|website=Scientific American|date=March 2003 |language=en|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>
*''Low Energy Ways to Observe High-Energy Phenomena'', by David B. Cline, was published in the September 1994 issue of Scientific American. Cline beings by introducing the concept of [[flavor-changing neutral current]]s (FCNCs), which is a class of interactions that change the flavor of [[fermion]]s without changing the charge, and are theorized to be caused by new and exotic particles that lie beyond the Standard Model.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/low-energy-ways-to-observe-high-ene/|title=Low-Energy Ways to Observe High-Energy Phenomena|website=Scientific American|date=September 1994 |language=en|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>
*''Beyond Truth and Beauty: A Fourth Family of Particles'',  by David B. Cline, was published in the August 1988 issue of Scientific American and explains why a fourth family of [[quark]]s and [[lepton]]s is likely to exist due to [[CP violation|charge-parity violation]] seen in certain particle decays.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/beyond-truth-and-beauty-a-fourth-fa/|title=Beyond Truth and Beauty: A Fourth Family of Particles|website=Scientific American|date=August 1988 |language=en|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>
*''The Search for Intermediate Vector Bosons'', by David B. Cline, [[Carlo Rubbia]] and [[Simon van der Meer]] and published in the March 1982 issue of Scientific American, dives into the theorized massive elementary particles that serve to carry the [[Weak interaction|weak nuclear force]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-search-for-intermediate-vector/|title=The Search for Intermediate Vector Bosons|website=Scientific American|date=March 1982 |language=en|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>
*''The Search for New Families of Elementary Particles'', by David B. Cline, [[Alfred K. Mann]], and [[Carlo Rubbia]] and published in the January 1976 edition of Scientific American, describes the discovery of a particle that exhibits some hitherto unobserved property of matter that has researchers believing it doesn't fit in the established families.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-search-for-new-families-of-elem/|title=The Search for New Families of Elementary Particles|website=Scientific American|date=January 1976 |language=en|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>
*''The Detection of Weak Neutral Currents'', written by David B. Cline, [[Alfred K. Mann]], and [[Carlo Rubbia]], was an article published in the December 1974 issue of Scientific American highlighting the previously unobserved interactions from the [[W and Z bosons|W and Z boson]] that support a link between the [[Weak interaction|weak nuclear force]] and the [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetic force]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-detection-of-neutral-weak-curre/|title=The Detection of Neutral Weak Currents|website=Scientific American|date=December 1974 |language=en|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>
*''High-Energy Scattering'', by David B. Cline and Vernon D. Barger and published in the December 1967 edition of Scientific American explains what it takes to study the properties of [[Elementary particle|fundamental particles]]. By accelerating and colliding particles at high energies, researchers are able to observe the fundamental particles that composed the previous particles using a [[bubble chamber]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/high-energy-scattering/|title=High-Energy Scattering|website=Scientific American|date=December 1967 |language=en|access-date=2020-01-20}}</ref>

== References in Media ==

=== Last Documented Interview ===
David Cline's last documented interview was a part of director Vincent Tran's movie ''One Under the Sun'' (2017), a science-fiction movie in which "The sole survivor of a doomed space mission attempts to reunite with her terminally ill daughter. The government, however, believes she's returned to earth with an extraordinary power and orders her confined to a secret facility".<ref>{{Citation|title=One Under the Sun|url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt5110386/|access-date=2020-01-19}}</ref> The movie captured Cline's last documented interview, in which he discusses religion, the origin of the universe and how it relates to the origin of life, and the [[Higgs boson]]. He most notably considers the journey of a universe consisting only of elementary particles, and how we can study these elementary particles to investigate the origins of the universe and the [[Big Bang|big bang]].<ref name=":6">{{Citation|title=One Under the Sun {{!}} Interview David Cline (1933 - 2015)| date=10 January 2017 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1MLwWUwjBDQ|language=en|access-date=2020-01-19}}</ref> <br />He ponders on the idea that the universe was self-created, following [[Stephen Hawking]]'s argument which he popularized in his book "[[The Grand Design (book)|The Grand Design]]". Cline argued that the [[Higgs boson]] must be present at the beginning of the universe in order to account for the mass of matter, and without it, the universe could not have been self-created. He admits that this topic borders on the line of religion because of the lack of proof and its ability to undermine other theories.<ref name=":6" /> 
Concerning the origin of life, Cline sets out on connecting the [[Higgs boson]] to the big bang. He begins by stating the coincidence that all [[amino acid]]s are [[Chirality (chemistry)|left handed molecules]] and all [[nucleic acid]]s are [[Chirality (chemistry)|right handed molecules]]. He argues that life could have been created by any combinations of the amino-acids found on earth, but life settled on the 21 acids by chance. Cline mentions a meteor found in Australia, referencing the [[Murchison meteorite]]. He explains that because the meteor had a large volume, the core of the meteor was left unharmed from the radiation that had damaged the outer layers. This led to the great discovery of over 70 new amino acids, different from the ones previously found on earth. He uses this example to illustrate how many different combinations of amino-acids could have led to the formation of life, leading to the necessity of a common origin of life. [[Supernova]] explosions emit 10<sup>57</sup> neutrinos, which can induce a left-handedness in the surrounding matter, and due to the Supernova Neutrino Amino Acid Processing model,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Boyd|first1=Richard N.|last2=Famiano|first2=Michael A.|last3=Onaka|first3=Takashi|last4=Kajino|first4=Toshitaka|date=2018-03-21|title=Sites that Can Produce Left-handed Amino Acids in the Supernova Neutrino Amino Acid Processing Model|url=http://stacks.iop.org/0004-637X/856/i=1/a=26?key=crossref.5564a5ada3b059be0eb0d55d715bd50e|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|volume=856|issue=1|page=26|doi=10.3847/1538-4357/aaad5f|issn=1538-4357|arxiv=1802.08285|bibcode=2018ApJ...856...26B|s2cid=118971100 |doi-access=free }}</ref> leading to the generation of left-handed amino acids, dubbing them amino-acid factories. Cline concludes by stating his belief that all amino acids in our body came from outer space, connecting the origin of life to the early days of the universe.<ref name=":6" />

=== Books ===

==== Telescope in the Ice ====
''The Telescope in the Ice: Inventing a New Astronomy at the South Pole'', by [[Mark Bowen (writer)|Mark Bowen]] draws on his involvement in the [[IceCube Neutrino Observatory|IceCube]] project in Antarctica. David Cline was mentioned in the book due to his role in the project as well. Cline was involved in the search for high-energy cosmic neutrinos through the [[IceCube Neutrino Observatory]] at the [[Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station|Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station]]. He was brought on the project for his expertise in neutrino interactions, and was said to be one of the project's founder's, [[Francis Halzen]], most important mentors.<ref name=":5" />

==== Nobel Dreams ====
''Nobel Dreams: Power, Deceit and the Ultimate Experiment'', by [[Gary Taubes]] mentions Cline for his contributions as a collaborator to the [[UA1 experiment|UA1]] and [[UA2 experiment|UA2]] experiments; the former eventually found the [[W and Z bosons]], and then won the award the book was named after.

== Personal life ==
David Cline married twice. He died on June 27, 2015, at UCLA Medical Center, following a heart attack on campus the previous afternoon. He  is survived by five children and eight grandchildren.<ref name="pa.ucla.edu"/>
